source.name: ASTRA chemistry practice set
source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: Lavoisier’s law of conservation of mass states that, in a closed chemical change, the total mass of reactants compared with products is
questions.explanation: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in ordinary chemical reactions, so reactant and product masses match.

questions.stem: Proust’s law of definite proportions says that a given pure compound always contains the same elements combined in
options: a ratio that depends on how it was prepared
questions.explanation: The elemental composition by mass of a pure compound is constant, independent of source.

questions.stem: Dalton’s law of multiple proportions applies when two elements form more than one compound. The masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other stand in
questions.explanation: Different compounds of the same two elements show small-integer mass ratios for one element at fixed mass of the other.

questions.stem: Gay-Lussac’s law of combining volumes concerns gases measured at the same temperature and pressure. Their reacting volumes are
options: inversely proportional to molar mass only
questions.explanation: Gaseous reactants and products combine or form in small integer volume ratios under identical T and P.

questions.stem: Avogadro’s hypothesis, used with Gay-Lussac’s volume data, states that equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain
options: equal numbers of atoms in every case
one mole only if the gas is monatomic
questions.explanation: Equal gas volumes at the same T and P hold the same number of molecules, which explains simple volume ratios.

questions.stem: The law of reciprocal proportions (Richter) compares how two elements A and B each combine with a fixed mass of a third element C. The A:B mass ratio so obtained is
options: the same as, or a simple multiple of, the ratio in which A and B combine with each other
independent of any compound of A with B
questions.explanation: Masses of A and B that combine with a fixed mass of C match the combining ratio of A with B, or a simple multiple of it.

questions.stem: In a sealed tube, 12 g of carbon is burnt completely in 32 g of oxygen to give carbon dioxide only. The mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ that must be collected is
questions.explanation: Conservation of mass requires $12 + 32 = 44$ g of product when nothing else is formed.

questions.stem: Carbon forms two oxides. With 12 g of carbon, one oxide contains 16 g of oxygen and the other contains 32 g of oxygen. These oxygen masses illustrate multiple proportions because their ratio is
questions.explanation: For a fixed 12 g of carbon the oxygen masses 16 g and 32 g stand in the simple ratio 1 : 2.

questions.stem: At the same T and P, two volumes of hydrogen gas combine with one volume of oxygen gas to give steam. The volume of steam formed, if measured under the same conditions, is
questions.explanation: Gay-Lussac’s ratio for $2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$ is 2 : 1 : 2 by volume.

questions.stem: Two oxides of copper are analysed. In the first, 6.35 g of copper is combined with 0.80 g of oxygen; in the second, 6.35 g of copper is combined with 1.60 g of oxygen. The oxygen masses that combine with the same mass of copper are in the ratio
questions.explanation: Fixed 6.35 g Cu takes 0.80 g then 1.60 g of oxygen, a 1 : 2 ratio, which is Dalton’s multiple-proportion test.

questions.stem: Avogadro’s constant $N_A$ is accepted as approximately
questions.explanation: One mole contains $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ specified elementary entities.

questions.stem: The SI mole is defined so that 12 g of the carbon-12 nuclide contains
questions.explanation: By definition, 12 g of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ is 1 mol and therefore holds $N_A$ atoms.

questions.stem: The amount of substance $n$ and the number of elementary entities $N$ are linked by
questions.explanation: Dividing the particle count by Avogadro’s constant converts it to moles.

questions.stem: One unified atomic mass unit (1 u) is defined as
options: the mass of one hydrogen atom
one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
the mass of one oxygen-16 atom
questions.explanation: The u (or amu) is $1/12$ of the mass of a single $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ atom.

questions.stem: Gram-atomic mass of an element is the mass, in grams, of
options: Avogadro’s number of molecules of any compound
questions.explanation: The gram-atomic mass is numerically equal to the atomic mass and is the mass of $N_A$ atoms.

questions.stem: At 273 K and 1 atm (classic STP), the molar volume of an ideal gas is taken in Intermediate tables as
questions.explanation: One mole of ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at 273 K and 1 atm.

questions.stem: A pair of samples that must contain the same number of molecules is
options: 22.4 L of $\mathrm{H_2}$ at STP and 11.2 L of $\mathrm{He}$ at STP
questions.explanation: Equal amounts in moles contain equal numbers of molecules, whatever the formula.

questions.stem: Half a mole of dioxygen molecules contains oxygen atoms numbering
questions.explanation: Each $\mathrm{O_2}$ molecule has two atoms, so $0.5\,N_A$ molecules hold $N_A$ atoms.

questions.stem: The numerical value $1.66 \times 10^{-24}$ g is the approximate mass of
questions.explanation: 1 u $\approx 1.66 \times 10^{-24}$ g, which is $1/N_A$ grams.

questions.stem: Twelve grams of carbon-12 and eighteen grams of water both represent
options: one mole of the stated substance
questions.explanation: 12 g of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ is 1 mol of atoms; 18 g of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ is 1 mol of molecules.

questions.stem: If a flask holds $3.011 \times 10^{23}$ molecules of nitrogen, the amount of $\mathrm{N_2}$ in that flask is
One mole of helium atoms and one mole of hydrogen molecules agree in
options: number of elementary entities counted as ‘one mole’
questions.explanation: A mole always contains $N_A$ of the named entities: He atoms or $\mathrm{H_2}$ molecules.

questions.stem: An STP sample of ammonia occupying 11.2 L contains molecules numbering
questions.explanation: 11.2 L at STP is 0.50 mol, so the molecule count is $0.50\,N_A = 3.011 \times 10^{23}$.

questions.stem: A 4.4 g portion of carbon dioxide is analysed for atoms. Taking $M(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 44\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, the total number of atoms present is
questions.explanation: 4.4 g is 0.10 mol of $\mathrm{CO_2}$; each molecule has 3 atoms, giving $0.30\,N_A$ atoms.

questions.stem: Compare 16 g of methane with 16 g of dioxygen. The sample that holds more molecules is
options: neither; the molecule counts are equal
questions.explanation: 16 g $\mathrm{CH_4}$ is 1.0 mol of molecules; 16 g $\mathrm{O_2}$ is only 0.50 mol, so methane has twice as many molecules.

questions.stem: A gas burette delivers 2.24 L of hydrogen, measured at STP. The amount of $\mathrm{H_2}$ collected is
questions.explanation: Moles $= 2.24 / 22.4 = 0.10$ mol at STP.

questions.stem: A sealed ampoule contains $3.011 \times 10^{23}$ molecules of dinitrogen. The mass of that $\mathrm{N_2}$ sample is
questions.explanation: The count is 0.50 mol; mass $= 0.50 \times 28 = 14$ g.

questions.stem: Eight grams of dioxygen and seven grams of dinitrogen are compared atom by atom. The two samples contain
options: equal numbers of molecules and equal numbers of atoms
equal numbers of molecules but different numbers of atoms
different numbers of molecules but equal numbers of atoms
neither equal molecules nor equal atoms
questions.explanation: Both are 0.25 mol of diatomic molecules, so both have $0.25\,N_A$ molecules and $0.50\,N_A$ atoms.

questions.stem: A 0.25 mol sample of $\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2}$ is examined. The number of oxygen atoms in the sample is
questions.explanation: Each formula unit has 8 oxygen atoms, so $0.25 \times 8 = 2.00$ mol of O atoms, i.e. $2.00\,N_A$.

questions.stem: Among 8 g $\mathrm{O_2}$, 7 g $\mathrm{N_2}$, 4 g $\mathrm{He}$ and 9 g $\mathrm{H_2O}$, the largest number of atoms is present in
questions.explanation: Atom amounts are 0.50, 0.50, 1.0 and 1.5 mol respectively; 9 g water therefore has the most atoms.

questions.stem: Using H = 1, S = 32 and O = 16, the molar mass of sulphuric acid $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ is
Calcium carbonate $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16) has a formula mass of
The percentage by mass of oxygen in water is closest to
questions.explanation: Oxygen contributes 16 of the 18 g in one mole of $\mathrm{H_2O}$, i.e. $16/18 \times 100 = 88.9\%$.

questions.stem: In methane, the mass percent of carbon (C = 12, H = 1) works out to
questions.explanation: Carbon is 12 g in 16 g of $\mathrm{CH_4}$, so $12/16 \times 100 = 75\%$.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide is assigned a molecular mass of 44 u because that value equals
questions.explanation: One C and two O atoms give $12 + 32 = 44$ u.

questions.stem: Ammonia’s gram-molecular mass, with N = 14 and H = 1, is
Hydrogen’s share of the mass of water, expressed as a percentage, is
questions.explanation: Two grams of H in 18 g of water give $2/18 \times 100 = 11.1\%$.

questions.stem: Solid sodium hydroxide (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1) has a molar mass of
The calcium content of pure $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (M = 100 g mol$^{-1}$) by mass percent is
questions.explanation: 40 g of Ca in 100 g of carbonate is a 40% calcium assay.

questions.stem: Urea, $\mathrm{NH_2CONH_2}$ (M = 60 g mol$^{-1}$), is valued as a fertiliser for nitrogen. The nitrogen mass percent in urea is
questions.explanation: Two N atoms contribute 28 g in 60 g, so $28/60 \times 100 = 46.7\%$.

questions.stem: Potassium chlorate $\mathrm{KClO_3}$ (M = 122.5 g mol$^{-1}$) releases oxygen on heating. Oxygen’s mass percent in $\mathrm{KClO_3}$ is nearest to
questions.explanation: Three oxygen atoms weigh 48 g in 122.5 g, giving $48/122.5 \times 100 \approx 39.2\%$.

questions.stem: From a 50 g laboratory sample of pure $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, the mass of oxygen that can be accounted for in the formula is
questions.explanation: Oxygen is 48% of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, so $0.48 \times 50 = 24$ g.

questions.stem: Blue vitriol $\mathrm{CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O}$ (M = 249.5 g mol$^{-1}$) loses its water of crystallisation on strong heating. The mass percent of water in the pentahydrate is nearest to
questions.explanation: Five water molecules weigh 90 g in 249.5 g, so $90/249.5 \times 100 \approx 36.1\%$.

questions.stem: Haematite $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ (M = 160 g mol$^{-1}$) is 70% iron by mass. An 80 g ore sample that is 80% pure $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ (rest gangue) contains iron weighing
questions.explanation: Pure oxide in the ore is $0.80 \times 80 = 64$ g; iron in that oxide is $0.70 \times 64 = 44.8$ g.

questions.stem: The empirical formula of a compound is the formula that shows
options: the actual number of atoms in one molecule
the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms present
only the metals in the compound
the percentage by mass of each element
questions.explanation: Empirical formulae give the smallest integer atom ratio, not necessarily the molecular formula.

questions.stem: A molecular formula is related to the empirical formula by a positive integer $n$ such that
questions.explanation: $n = M / $ (empirical formula mass), and the molecular formula is that multiple of the empirical set.

questions.stem: Benzene has molecular formula $\mathrm{C_6H_6}$. Its empirical formula is therefore
questions.explanation: Dividing $\mathrm{C_6H_6}$ by 6 gives the simplest ratio CH.

questions.stem: Glucose, $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$, reduces to the empirical set
questions.explanation: Each subscript is divisible by 6, leaving CH$_2$O.

questions.stem: Hydrogen peroxide $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$ has the empirical formula
questions.explanation: The simplest H : O ratio in hydrogen peroxide is 1 : 1, written HO.

questions.stem: An organic gas has empirical formula $\mathrm{CH_2}$ and a molar mass of 56 g mol$^{-1}$. Its molecular formula is
questions.explanation: Empirical mass is 14; $n = 56/14 = 4$, so the molecule is $\mathrm{C_4H_8}$.

questions.stem: The integer $n$ that converts an empirical formula into the molecular formula is calculated as
questions.explanation: $n = M / E$, then each empirical subscript is multiplied by $n$.

questions.stem: For an ionic solid such as $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$, the formula written on the bottle is already
options: a molecular formula that can be halved
the empirical formula of the compound
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds are represented by the simplest ratio of ions, which is the empirical formula.

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon analyses as 80% carbon and 20% hydrogen by mass. Its empirical formula is
A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O. The empirical formula matching these percentages is
questions.explanation: Moles C : H : O $= 3.33 : 6.7 : 3.33 = 1 : 2 : 1$, which is $\mathrm{CH_2O}$.

questions.stem: A vapour has empirical formula CH and a vapour density corresponding to $M = 78$ g mol$^{-1}$. The molecular formula of the vapour is
questions.explanation: Empirical mass 13; $n = 78/13 = 6$, giving $\mathrm{C_6H_6}$.

questions.stem: An iron oxide is 70% Fe and 30% O by mass (Fe = 56, O = 16). The oxide’s empirical formula is
A hydrocarbon is 85.7% carbon, the rest hydrogen. The empirical formula of that hydrocarbon is
A chloro-compound is 24.24% C, 4.04% H and 71.72% Cl. Its molar mass is 99 g mol$^{-1}$. The molecular formula is
questions.explanation: Empirical moles give $\mathrm{CH_2Cl}$ (E = 49.5); $n = 99/49.5 = 2$, so $\mathrm{C_2H_4Cl_2}$.

questions.stem: In the Haber equation $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_3}$, each mole of nitrogen that reacts consumes hydrogen amounting to
questions.explanation: The coefficient of $\mathrm{H_2}$ is 3, so the mole ratio N$_2$ : H$_2$ is 1 : 3.

questions.stem: According to $2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}$, complete use of 1 mol of oxygen produces water equal to
questions.explanation: One mole of $\mathrm{O_2}$ corresponds to two moles of $\mathrm{H_2O}$.

questions.stem: Thermal decomposition $\mathrm{CaCO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}$ is 1 : 1 : 1 in moles. From 1 mol of limestone the carbon dioxide obtained is
questions.explanation: Each mole of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ yields one mole of $\mathrm{CO_2}$.

questions.stem: The laboratory oxygen preparation $2\mathrm{KClO_3} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{O_2}$ gives, from 2 mol of chlorate, oxygen amounting to
questions.explanation: The O$_2$ coefficient is 3 when 2 mol of $\mathrm{KClO_3}$ decompose.

questions.stem: Complete combustion $\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2}$ links carbon and carbon dioxide in the mole ratio
questions.explanation: Coefficients of C and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ are both 1.

questions.stem: Magnesium burns as $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$. Oxygen amounting to 1 mol therefore requires magnesium equal to
questions.explanation: Two moles of Mg are needed for each mole of $\mathrm{O_2}$.

questions.stem: Methane burns as $\mathrm{CH_4} + 2\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$. The oxygen-to-methane mole ratio demanded by the equation is
questions.explanation: Two moles of $\mathrm{O_2}$ are required for every mole of $\mathrm{CH_4}$.

questions.stem: Contact-process oxidation $2\mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{SO_3}$ converts 1 mol of oxygen into sulphur trioxide amounting to
questions.explanation: One mole of $\mathrm{O_2}$ produces two moles of $\mathrm{SO_3}$.

questions.stem: Aluminium burns in oxygen: $4\mathrm{Al} + 3\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$. Four moles of aluminium therefore form alumina equal to
questions.explanation: The product coefficient is 2 when 4 mol of Al react.

questions.stem: Hydrogen chloride is formed by $\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl}$. One mole of hydrogen gas yields HCl equal to
questions.explanation: The HCl coefficient is 2 for each mole of $\mathrm{H_2}$.

questions.stem: Propane burns as $\mathrm{C_3H_8} + 5\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{CO_2} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}$. Complete combustion of 2 mol of propane releases carbon dioxide amounting to
questions.explanation: Each mole of $\mathrm{C_3H_8}$ gives 3 mol $\mathrm{CO_2}$, so 2 mol give 6 mol.

questions.stem: A Haber converter is charged with 10 mol of hydrogen and surplus nitrogen. The maximum ammonia that can form is
questions.explanation: From $3\mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_3}$, 10 mol H$_2$ produce $(10 \times 2)/3 = 20/3 \approx 6.67$ mol NH$_3$.

questions.stem: Two moles of $\mathrm{KClO_3}$ are fully decomposed to KCl and O$_2$. The STP volume of oxygen collected is
questions.explanation: 2 mol chlorate give 3 mol O$_2$; $3 \times 22.4 = 67.2$ L at STP.

questions.stem: A bunsen flame consumes 16 g of methane completely (M = 16 g mol$^{-1}$). The STP volume of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ produced is
questions.explanation: 16 g is 1 mol $\mathrm{CH_4}$ and gives 1 mol $\mathrm{CO_2}$, which occupies 22.4 L at STP.

questions.stem: A 50 g charge of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ (M = 100 g mol$^{-1}$) is heated until decomposition is complete. The lime $\mathrm{CaO}$ (M = 56 g mol$^{-1}$) obtained weighs
questions.explanation: 0.50 mol of carbonate yields 0.50 mol of CaO, i.e. 28 g.

questions.stem: Ethane burns as $2\mathrm{C_2H_6} + 7\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{CO_2} + 6\mathrm{H_2O}$. A 15 g sample of ethane (M = 30) is burnt in 64 g of oxygen. The mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ formed and the unused $\mathrm{O_2}$ are
questions.explanation: 0.50 mol ethane needs 1.75 mol (56 g) O$_2$ and makes 1.0 mol (44 g) CO$_2$; 64 − 56 = 8 g O$_2$ remains.

questions.stem: After a reaction stops, the starting material that is left unused is called the
questions.explanation: The excess reagent remains because the other reactant ran out first.

questions.stem: One mole of $\mathrm{H_2}$ is mixed with one mole of $\mathrm{O_2}$ and sparked to form water. The reactant that is used up completely is
questions.explanation: Water needs H$_2$ : O$_2$ = 2 : 1, so 1 mol H$_2$ is finished while 0.5 mol O$_2$ is still unused.

questions.stem: A flask is charged with 1 mol of $\mathrm{N_2}$ and 1 mol of $\mathrm{H_2}$ for the Haber reaction. Ammonia production is limited by
questions.explanation: The 1 : 3 nitrogen-to-hydrogen requirement means 1 mol H$_2$ is exhausted long before the nitrogen.

questions.stem: Two moles of carbon are heated with one mole of oxygen to give only $\mathrm{CO_2}$. The reagent that decides the amount of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is
questions.explanation: Each mole of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ needs 1 mol O$_2$; only 1 mol O$_2$ is supplied, so oxygen limits.

questions.stem: Equal molar amounts of $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ are allowed to form HCl. At the end of the reaction
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl}$ uses the two gases in a 1 : 1 mole ratio.

questions.stem: Three moles of magnesium ribbon are burnt in one mole of oxygen. Formation of $\mathrm{MgO}$ is limited by
questions.explanation: $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2}$ needs Mg : O$_2$ = 2 : 1; 1 mol O$_2$ can consume only 2 mol Mg, so oxygen limits.

questions.stem: The quantity of product that can form in a given run is fixed by
options: the reagent present in greater mass, always
the reagent that is consumed first
the reagent with the larger molar mass
questions.explanation: The limiting reagent is used up first and therefore caps the product.

questions.stem: If a balanced equation is 1 : 1 and the two reactants are supplied in unequal moles, the leftover substance is
options: the reactant that was supplied in smaller moles
the reactant that was supplied in larger moles
questions.explanation: The reactant present in fewer moles is limiting; the one in larger moles is excess and remains.

questions.stem: One mole of sulphur is burnt in two moles of oxygen to give only $\mathrm{SO_2}$. The unused oxygen at the end is
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{S} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO_2}$ uses 1 mol O$_2$, leaving 1 mol unused.

questions.stem: Aluminium and chlorine are mixed as 2 mol Al + 3 mol $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ to form $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ ($2\mathrm{Al} + 3\mathrm{Cl_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{AlCl_3}$). The limiting reagent is
questions.explanation: The supplied amounts match the 2 : 3 coefficients, so both finish together.

questions.stem: Four grams of hydrogen (M = 2) are sparked with 32 g of oxygen (M = 32) to form water. The mass of water that can form is
questions.explanation: 2 mol H$_2$ and 1 mol O$_2$ match $2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$; both are used and give 2 mol (36 g) of water.

questions.stem: A converter is loaded with 14 g of nitrogen and 6 g of hydrogen for ammonia synthesis. The reagent that runs out first is
questions.explanation: 14 g N$_2$ is 0.50 mol and would need 1.5 mol H$_2$; 6 g H$_2$ is 3.0 mol, so nitrogen is consumed first.

questions.stem: Twelve grams of carbon are heated with 16 g of oxygen, forming only $\mathrm{CO_2}$. The mass of carbon dioxide obtained is
questions.explanation: 1.0 mol C needs 1.0 mol (32 g) O$_2$; only 0.50 mol O$_2$ is present, so 0.50 mol (22 g) of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ forms.

questions.stem: Eight grams of hydrogen are burnt in 32 g of oxygen. After water has formed, the unused hydrogen weighs
questions.explanation: 1 mol O$_2$ consumes 2 mol (4 g) H$_2$; 8 g H$_2$ was supplied, so 4 g of hydrogen remains.

questions.stem: Two moles of $\mathrm{SO_2}$ are oxidised with two moles of $\mathrm{O_2}$ to $\mathrm{SO_3}$. The oxygen left unreacted is
questions.explanation: $2\mathrm{SO_2}$ need only 1 mol O$_2$; of the 2 mol supplied, 1 mol remains.

questions.stem: Marble chips (25 g $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, M = 100) are treated with 14.6 g of HCl (M = 36.5) according to $\mathrm{CaCO_3} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}$. The mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ that can escape is
questions.explanation: 0.25 mol carbonate would need 0.50 mol HCl, but only 0.40 mol HCl is present, so HCl limits and $0.20$ mol (8.8 g) of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ forms.

questions.stem: Theoretical yield is the mass of product calculated by assuming that
options: the limiting reagent is completely converted as the equation is written
questions.explanation: Theoretical yield is the stoichiometric maximum from the limiting reagent.

questions.stem: Percentage yield is obtained from the relation
questions.explanation: Percent yield $= (\text{actual yield}/\text{theoretical yield}) \times 100$.

questions.stem: When the mass collected on the filter equals the mass predicted from the equation, the percentage yield is
questions.explanation: Actual = theoretical gives a 100% yield.

questions.stem: In the school laboratory the isolated product is usually lighter than the theoretical mass because of
options: incomplete reaction, side products and handling losses
the law of conservation of mass being false
questions.explanation: Real recoveries suffer from incomplete conversion, competing reactions and transfer losses.

questions.stem: A statement that the yield is 100% means that
options: every mole of limiting reagent appeared in the isolated product as written
questions.explanation: A quantitative isolation matching the stoichiometric prediction is a 100% yield.

questions.stem: A preparation is calculated to give 50 g of crystals; the dried crop actually weighs 40 g. The percentage yield of that run is
A process is known to run at 80% yield. If the equation predicts 25 g of product, the mass a student should expect to isolate is
questions.explanation: Actual $= 0.80 \times 25 = 20$ g.

questions.stem: Excess oxygen is used to burn 4.0 g of hydrogen. The equation predicts 36 g of water, but only 27 g is condensed. The percentage yield of water is
questions.explanation: 4.0 g H$_2$ is 2.0 mol and can give 2.0 mol (36 g) of water; $27/36 \times 100 = 75\%$.

questions.stem: An uncombined free element, whether atom or molecule, is assigned an oxidation number of
questions.explanation: The oxidation number of an element in its elemental form is zero.

questions.stem: Except in peroxides, superoxides and $\mathrm{OF_2}$, oxygen in compounds is assigned the oxidation number
questions.explanation: The common oxidation number of oxygen in oxides and oxo-salts is $-2$.

questions.stem: Hydrogen combined with a non-metal is assigned the oxidation number
questions.explanation: In hydrides of non-metals (HCl, H$_2$O, NH$_3$) hydrogen is $+1$.

questions.stem: In their compounds the alkali metals (Li, Na, K, …) show the oxidation number
questions.explanation: Group 1 metals lose one valence electron and are $+1$ in compounds.

questions.stem: Fluorine, being the most electronegative element, has in all its compounds the oxidation number
questions.explanation: Fluorine is always $-1$ in compounds.

questions.stem: In hydrogen chloride the oxidation number of chlorine is
questions.explanation: H is $+1$ and the molecule is neutral, so Cl is $-1$.

questions.stem: Sulphur in hydrogen sulphide $\mathrm{H_2S}$ has the oxidation number
questions.explanation: Two hydrogens at $+1$ force sulphur to $-2$ in the neutral molecule.

questions.stem: Nitrogen in ammonia $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is assigned the oxidation number
questions.explanation: Three hydrogens at $+1$ give nitrogen $-3$.

questions.stem: Carbon in methane $\mathrm{CH_4}$ carries the oxidation number
questions.explanation: Four hydrogens at $+1$ leave carbon at $-4$.

questions.stem: In hydrogen peroxide $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$ the oxidation number of each oxygen atom is
questions.explanation: Peroxidic oxygen is $-1$; two H at $+1$ and two O at $-1$ balance the molecule.

questions.stem: Sulphur in sulphuric acid $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ has the oxidation number
Chromium in potassium dichromate $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$ has the oxidation number
questions.explanation: $2(+1) + 2\mathrm{Cr} + 7(-2) = 0$ gives each Cr $= +6$.

questions.stem: Manganese in potassium permanganate $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ is assigned
questions.explanation: $+1 + \mathrm{Mn} + 4(-2) = 0$ gives Mn $= +7$.

questions.stem: Nitrogen in nitric acid $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ has the oxidation number
The average oxidation number of sulphur in sodium thiosulphate $\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3}$ is
questions.explanation: $2(+1) + 2\mathrm{S} + 3(-2) = 0$ gives $2\mathrm{S} = +4$, so each S averages $+2$.

questions.stem: In magnetite $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ iron is present in two oxidation states. The average oxidation number of iron in $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$ is
questions.explanation: Four oxide ions contribute $-8$; three Fe atoms share $+8$, so the average is $+8/3$ (one Fe$^{2+}$ and two Fe$^{3+}$).

questions.stem: Oxidation, in electronic language, is the process in which a species
questions.explanation: Loss of electrons raises the oxidation number and is oxidation.

questions.stem: Reduction is identified as a
questions.explanation: Gain of electrons lowers the oxidation number and is reduction.

questions.stem: An oxidising agent is the species that
questions.explanation: The oxidising agent accepts electrons and is reduced.

questions.stem: A reducing agent is the species that
questions.explanation: The reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidised.

questions.stem: When magnesium ribbon burns, $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$. The element that is oxidised is
questions.explanation: Mg goes from 0 to $+2$ (loses electrons) and is oxidised; oxygen is reduced.

questions.stem: In $\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + \mathrm{Cu}$, the reducing agent is
questions.explanation: Zinc metal loses electrons (0 to $+2$) and therefore reduces $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$.

questions.stem: A disproportionation reaction is one in which the same element is
options: left with an unchanged oxidation number
questions.explanation: Part of the element’s atoms rise in ON and part fall, as in $2\mathrm{H_2O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{O_2}$.

questions.stem: The combination $\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl}$ is classified as redox because
options: hydrogen is oxidised (0 to $+1$) and chlorine is reduced (0 to $-1$)
it is only an acid–base reaction

questions.stem: In acid, dichromate oxidises $\mathrm{H_2S}$ to sulphur: $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{H_2S} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{S} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}$. The coefficient 3 in front of $\mathrm{H_2S}$ appears because

questions.explanation: H$_2$S (S = $-2$ to 0) is a 2-electron reductant; Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ is a 6-electron oxidant, so three H$_2$S balance one dichromate.
